posts.quote: A RAINY DAY MEANT RUBBER BOOTS BY THE DOOR AND A PUDDLE ON EVERY CORNER WORTH JUMPING IN.
posts.caption: The minute the rain let up, Mom opened the front door and the boots were already lined up on the mat. Yellow ones, red ones, and a pair of hand-me-downs two sizes too big, stuffed with newspaper at the toes. You were out the door before she finished saying don't get wet. The puddle at the end of the street was deeper than you remembered, and the whole afternoon went to finding out exactly how deep. Somebody always went in over the top. You came home with squishy socks and a grin no towel could wipe off.
posts.first: There was a puddle at the corner of Elm and Fifth that never completely dried up, and we measured how much we'd grown by how far up our legs the water came. I remember the summer it finally stopped at my knee. Mom said that's the last time I'm buying you boots.

posts.quote: A BOX CAMERA, A FLASHBULB, AND A WEEK OF WAITING TO FIND OUT WHO BLINKED.
posts.caption: Every picture cost money, so somebody always said hold still and nobody did. Dad would crouch with the box camera held against his belly and count to three out loud. The flashbulb went off with a pop and left a purple dot floating in front of your eyes for five minutes. Then came the waiting. You dropped the film at the drugstore on Saturday and picked up the little envelope the following Saturday. Half the pictures were blurry, one had a thumb in it, and one was the best photograph our family ever took.
posts.first: We had one of those pictures on the piano for forty years. Everybody in it was looking in a different direction and my uncle's eyes were closed. Mom said it was the only honest photo we had. I'd give a lot to see it again.

posts.quote: DAD KICKED EACH TIRE BEFORE EVERY TRIP, AND THAT WAS THE WHOLE INSPECTION.
posts.caption: The suitcases were tied to the roof with rope, the cooler was jammed between the kids in back, and Mom had the road map folded to the wrong page. Dad walked around the car once, like a man inspecting troops. Front left tire, kick. Front right tire, kick. He nodded at the back ones from a distance as though they'd already passed. Then he got behind the wheel, tapped the dashboard twice for luck, and we were off. In all those years that method failed him exactly once, and we still talk about the afternoon in Ohio.
posts.first: He kicked those tires in the same shoes he mowed the lawn in. I remember thinking he knew something about rubber the rest of us didn't. Years later I asked him what he was checking for. He thought about it and said, mostly that they were still there.

posts.quote: Mom never said she was stressed. She just started cleaning the oven, and we all knew to stay out of the kitchen.
posts.first: When I was nine, Mom cleaned the oven three times in one week. Dad took us out for ice cream twice. Nobody said a word about it. By Friday the oven was spotless, the house was quiet, and Mom was humming at the sink again.

posts.quote: SHOW AND TELL / A ROCK, A BEETLE IN A MATCHBOX, AND A KID WHO WAS SURE HE HAD THE BEST ONE
posts.caption: Friday afternoon, the last half hour before the bell, the teacher said it was time. You had carried your treasure to school in a paper sack all day, guarding it from the boy behind you. One kid brought a rock from his grandfather's farm. One brought a tooth. One brought a beetle in a matchbox that ran out of patience before his turn came. Everybody clapped for every single one, and the beetle got the loudest cheer. Nobody remembers what the grown-up lesson was supposed to be. Everybody remembers the beetle.
posts.first: I brought my dad's old compass once. I held it up and told the class it always points north. The kid next to me raised his hand and asked what happens if you turn around. I still haven't come up with a good answer.

posts.quote: THE RECIPE BOX HAD A GREASE STAIN ON EVERY CARD, AND THE STAINS WERE HOW YOU KNEW WHICH ONES WERE GOOD.
posts.caption: Grandma kept hers in a green tin box on the shelf over the stove, right where the steam could get to it. The cards were soft as cloth from forty years of floury thumbs. Some were typed, some were in her mother's handwriting, and some just said Aunt Bea's, ask her, with no amounts at all. When you wanted to know whether a recipe was worth making, you didn't read it. You looked at the card. Butter spots meant a good one. A burn mark meant an old one. Brown rings from coffee cups meant the family had already voted.
posts.first: After Grandma passed, my cousins and I fought over that tin like it was gold. I got the card for her pound cake. It's so stained you can barely make out the word sugar. I've never made it as good, and I've stopped being upset about it.

posts.quote: THE PORCH SWING HAD ROOM FOR TWO AND OPINIONS ABOUT EVERYBODY WALKING BY.
posts.caption: Right after supper, when the dishes were done and the heat was finally breaking, the grown-ups drifted out to the front porch. The swing creaked on its chains with a rhythm you could set a clock by. Every person who passed got a wave, and every wave got a comment once they were out of earshot. Mrs. Dalton's new hat, the Peterson boy's loud car, who was home late from work. It wasn't gossip exactly. It was keeping track. You sat on the steps with a popsicle and learned more about the neighborhood than any newspaper could teach you.
posts.first: Our swing was Dad's project one summer. He hung it too high the first time, and Mom's feet never touched the ground. She sat there for a week without saying a word. Then one morning it was two inches lower and nobody ever mentioned it.

posts.quote: GRANDPA'S POCKETKNIFE AND A STICK OF WOOD WERE ALL THE ENTERTAINMENT AN AFTERNOON EVER NEEDED.
posts.caption: He sat on the bench under the big oak after lunch, took out the knife he'd carried since the war, and picked a stick the way another man might pick out a fishing rod. Nobody asked what he was making, because he didn't know yet either. The shavings curled up and dropped around his boots while he hummed something with no tune. Maybe it would turn into a whistle. Maybe a little bird, a spoon, or just a smaller stick. A grandkid always ended up beside him, handed the first shavings, and told not to touch the blade until he said.
posts.first: The first thing he ever made me was a whistle that sounded like a dying goose. Mom hid it within three weeks. I found it years later in her sewing drawer, and she told me she'd kept it on purpose.

posts.character: Values and work ethic (Grandpa's retirement plan)
posts.quote: Grandpa's whole retirement plan was a garden, a porch chair, and a very strong opinion about the neighbor's hedge.
posts.first: My grandfather and Mr. Pruitt feuded over a hedge for nineteen years. They also rode to church together every Sunday and fished every August. When Mr. Pruitt passed, Grandpa trimmed that hedge perfectly straight, and then he stood there looking at it for a long time.

posts.quote: THE ICEMAN / A BLOCK OF ICE ON HIS SHOULDER AND EVERY KID ON THE BLOCK RIGHT BEHIND HIS TRUCK
posts.caption: He came down the street twice a week in a green truck with a canvas cover, and every kid within earshot dropped what they were doing. He'd pull a big block from the back, clamp it with iron tongs, and swing it onto a leather pad on his shoulder like it weighed nothing. A card in the front window told him how much to bring. While he carried it inside, the kids picked through the sawdust in the truck bed for chips. Cold slivers on a hot afternoon. It was the best candy there was, and it didn't cost a thing.
posts.first: My aunt kept her icebox on the back porch long after the refrigerator came out because she swore it kept the butter better. She kept the card in the window too. The iceman stopped coming years earlier, but she never took it down.
